summaries.summary: Single-relation factoid questions are common in search query logs and community question answering websites, and KBs such as Freebase, DBpedia, or Wikidata can answer them after query reformulation.
Automatically mapping a natural language question such as Where was Barack Obama born? to its corresponding KB query remains challenging.

Three issues make learning this mapping non-trivial: paraphrases, unseen KB entries, and millions of entities and thousands of predicates, addressed by a compact character-level encoder-decoder framework.
The model uses an LSTM question encoder, character-level representations for questions, predicates and entities, and a semantic relevance interaction function instead of a large decoder output layer.
Without ensembles, the compact character-level model achieves 70.9% accuracy in Freebase2M and 70.3% in Freebase5M on SimpleQuestions, outperforming 62.7% and 63.9% by 8.2% and 6.4%.
The work is motivated by semantic-parsing for open-domain question answering, character-level language modeling, and encoder-decoder methods.
Semantic parsing translates a question into a structured KB query, with early lexicons for GeoQuery and recent frameworks for general knowledge bases such as Freebase.
Large-scale semantic parsing frameworks must generate queries for millions of entities and thousands of predicates, often using textual-description embeddings and a general interaction function.
Word-level embeddings may suffer from the OOV problem and often rely on significant data augmentation from sources such as Paralex, which contains 18 million question-paraphrase pairs.
Character-level modeling can handle the OOV issue and has been applied to information retrieval, machine translation, sentiment analysis, classification, and named entity recognition.
Encoder-decoder networks encode a source sequence with an RNN into a fixed-length vector and decode a target sequence, with applications across diverse domains.
The authors formulate question answering as decoding the KB query given the question and KB entries encoded in embedding spaces, optimized end-to-end in a unified encoder-decoder framework.
For single-relation question answering, the model decodes each question into a KB query with a topic entity and predicate, producing likelihood scores p(e_i, p_j|q).
As illustrated in Figure 1, the model consists of three components.
The details of each component are described in the following sections.
To encode the question, the authors take two steps.
The first step extracts one-hot encoding vectors for characters in the question, keeping space, punctuation and original cases without tokenization.
The second step feeds x_1,...,x_n left to right into a two-layer gated-feedback LSTM and keeps outputs s_1,...,s_n as question embeddings.
To encode an entity or predicate in the KB, the authors take two steps.
The first step extracts one-hot encoding vectors for characters in its English alias, x_1,...,x_n.
The second step feeds x_1,...,x_n into a temporal CNN with two alternating convolutional and fully-connected layers, followed by one fully-connected layer.
Here f(x_{1...n}) is an embedding vector of size N, W_3 has size R^{N × h}, conv is a temporal convolutional neural network, and max is temporal max pooling.
A CNN is used instead of an LSTM for computational efficiency, and two different CNNs encode entities and predicates because their styles differ significantly.
To generate the single topic entity and predicate forming the KB query, the decoder uses two key components.
An LSTM-based decoder with attention has hidden states h_i of dimensionality N, with initial hidden state h_0 set to the zero vector.
A pairwise semantic relevance function measures similarity between LSTM hidden units and entity or predicate candidate embeddings, returning the most likely candidate by similarity score.
The following two sections first describe the LSTM decoder with attention, followed by the semantic relevance function.
The attention-based LSTM decoder feeds context vector c_i and input vector v_i at each time step, with v_{<S>}=0 at i=1 and entity embeddings at i=2.
The context vector c_i represents attention-weighted question content and is recomputed at each time step using h_{i-1}, s_j, n, r, and m.
The attention distribution {α} is applied over each hidden unit s_j, with W_a ∈ R^{m × N}, U_a ∈ R^{m × r}, and v_a ∈ R^{1 × m}.
Because the KB has millions of entries, the model uses a relevance function with cosine-similarity metric cos(x_1, x_2) instead of a decoder output layer with millions of nodes.
Using this similarity metric, likelihoods of generating entity e_j and predicate p_k are defined with exp(λ cos(h_1,e_j)) and exp(λ cos(h_2,p_k)) normalized over candidates.
Here λ is a constant, h_1 and h_2 are LSTM hidden states at t=1 and t=2, and e_1,...,e_n and p_1,...,p_m are entity and predicate embeddings.
During inference candidates are candidate embeddings, while during training they include the true entity and predicate plus 50 randomly-sampled entities and 50 randomly-sampled predicates.
For each question q, candidate entities and predicates are fed through f(q, {e}, {p}), and the most likely (entity, predicate) pair is decoded by argmax P(e_i)*P(p_j).
The decoded most likely (entity, predicate) pair becomes the semantic parse.
Candidate entities are English aliases that are substrings of the question, filtered and ranked by facts, with top 10 entities per alias and all predicates for each candidate entity.
Learning maximizes the joint likelihood P(e_c) · P(p_c) of the correct entity and predicate pair from randomly sampled entities and predicates using back-propagation.
All parameters, including character-level embeddings, CNNs, and LSTMs, are learned jointly without pre-training and randomly initialized from a uniform distribution between -1/|l^i| and 1/|l^i|.
The SimpleQuestions dataset has 108,442 questions split into 75,910 train, 10,845 validation, and 21,687 test questions, with FB2M using 2M entities and FB5M using 5M entities.
MemNNs baselines use 76K training questions, 3K WebQuestions questions, 15M WikiAnswers paraphrases, and 11M or 12M generated questions, while the proposed models use only 76K questions.
The model uses LSTM encoder layers of size 200, decoder hidden layers of size 100, CNN hidden and output layers of 200 and 100, receptive field 4, λ=5, m=100, and RMSProp with learning rate 1e^{-4}.
Each predicate or entity is padded with three padding symbols P, a special start symbol, and a special end symbol, with the same padding applied to questions.
On SimpleQuestions, SQ accuracy is the percentage of correct KB queries; the single character-level model achieves 70.9% and 70.3% on FB2M and FB5M, outperforming state-of-art by 8.2% and 6.4%.
Ablation studies use random-sampling experiments with 200 entities and predicates from the test set as noise samples mixed with the gold entity and predicate.
The authors first explore word-level models as an alternative to character-level models for constructing embeddings for questions, entities and predicates.
Word-level and character-level models both reach around 80% predicate accuracy, but the word-level model predicts only 45% of entities accurately from the mixed set.
Character-level models achieve 96.6% accuracy in predicting the correct entity on the mixed set, demonstrating semantic representation of entities and matching of aliases with mentions.
Ablations compare single-layer and two-layer LSTMs and CNNs, finding that a two-layer LSTM boosts joint accuracy by over 6%, mostly through improved predicate predictions.
Figure 2 visualizes attention distributions over question characters during decoding, with blue curves for entity generation and green curves for predicate generation.
Attention distributions typically peak at empty spaces, indicating that the character-level model learns spaces define endings of complete linguistic units.
Entity attention distributions are usually less sharp and span longer word portions than predicate attention distributions, as shown in Figure 2a.
A character-level model can identify entities with unseen English aliases, such as phrenology, apparently learning that words ending with nology are likely entity mentions.
Figure 2d shows attention to disjoint question regions, predicate attention peaks at padding symbols, and university helps identify both entity and predicate.
Among 50 sampled wrong KB queries, 46 had similar predicate aliases, 21 had wrong entities, and 18 had wrong entity and predicate.
The proposed character-level, attention-based encoder-decoder model improved state-of-the-art accuracy on SimpleQuestions using much less data and robustly handles unseen entities.
